pricing.title: Anthropic Claude Model Pricing
pricing.description: Anthropic API rates per million tokens (USD). Use % as wildcard in patterns. Some models have a time-limited introductory rate (shown in violet); usage on or before its cutoff date is billed at that rate, and usage after it at the standard rate.
pricing.introRatesHint: Leave the date empty for no promo
pricing.introUntilInvalid: Introductory cutoff must be a YYYY-MM-DD date
pricing.validationRequired: Pattern and display name are required

tooltip.title: How model pricing works
tooltip.howItWorksBody: When a session reports usage, the dashboard finds the first pricing rule whose pattern matches the model id and multiplies (input tokens / 1M) and (output tokens / 1M) by the rates below to compute cost. Rules are evaluated top-to-bottom - the first match wins.
tooltip.patternsBody: Patterns are SQL-style globs. % is a wildcard that matches any characters. For example: claude-opus-4-7% matches every model id that starts with claude-opus-4-7 (e.g. claude-opus-4-7, claude-opus-4-7-20260101). claude-%-haiku matches any haiku variant. An exact id like claude-sonnet-4-6 only matches itself.
tooltip.manualUpdatesBody: Anthropic publishes pricing changes on their website - there is no live feed. When a new model launches or rates change, edit the matching rule (or add a new one above the catch-all) so newly recorded sessions are costed correctly. Already-stored sessions keep the price that was applied at ingest time.
tooltip.apiPricingBody: These are pay-as-you-go API rates. If you use Claude Code on a subscription plan (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise), your actual cost is a flat monthly fee, not per-token - so these figures will usually be higher than what you really pay. Treat the costs here as a usage estimate for reference, not a bill.

gpt.title: OpenAI GPT Model Pricing
gpt.description: Published OpenAI API rates for Codex usage. Standard requests use Short rates at or below 272K input tokens and Long rates above 272K; Fast mode uses its own rate card. USD per 1M tokens.

tooltip.title: How GPT pricing works
tooltip.howItWorksBody: Every amount is USD per 1M tokens. Standard Codex requests use Short rates at or below 272K input tokens and Long rates above 272K. Fast mode uses its own rate card. Fresh input, cached input, cache writes, and output are priced separately.
tooltip.patternsBody: Patterns use SQL-style % wildcards. The dashboard evaluates the most specific model patterns first and uses the first rule that matches the reported model id.
tooltip.manualUpdatesBody: OpenAI publishes API pricing changes on its website; there is no live feed. Update or add a matching rule when models or rates change so newly recorded usage is priced correctly.
tooltip.apiPricingBody: An em dash means OpenAI does not publish that context or Fast-mode rate. Matching usage is marked unpriced instead of being estimated. These are pay-as-you-go API rates for reference, not subscription-plan billing.

import.title: Import History
import.providerHint: Choose the local agent history you want to bring into this dashboard.
import.backupProviderNote: Dashboard exports can contain Claude Code and Codex data. Restore merges every provider included in the export.
import.description: Bring existing Claude Code sessions into the dashboard. Token counts, per-model cost, compactions, subagents, tool uses, and turn durations are reconstructed from the original JSONL transcripts - identical to how live sessions are captured.
import.scopeNote: This import processes only Claude Code transcripts. It never changes your Codex history or either CLI configuration.
import.accuracyNote: Re-running is safe. Sessions are deduplicated by session ID, and compaction baselines ensure token totals never double-count.
import.stepLocateBody: Every Claude Code session is stored as a JSONL transcript under the projects folder. Each subfolder is named after the working directory where the session started (slashes replaced with dashes).
import.stepArchiveBody: To move history from another machine, archive the whole folder first, then copy it over (AirDrop, scp, USB, cloud storage):
import.stepChooseBody: Rescan the default location, point at any folder you've extracted history into, or upload files/archives directly.
import.stepVerifyBody: After import, open Analytics → Cost to confirm the breakdown. Re-importing the same session is always safe.
import.modeFolderDesc: Scan any directory on this machine for JSONL transcripts (walks subfolders).
import.modeUploadDesc: Drop JSONL files or an archive (.zip / .tar.gz) directly into the browser.
import.modeBackupDesc: Import a dashboard export (.json) from Export data — merge another machine's history in.
import.backupHint: Drop an export .json here or click to select
import.backupSub: The file produced by the Export data button (top of Settings)
import.folderHelper: Absolute path. Tilde (~) is expanded. Subfolders are scanned recursively.
import.dropzoneHint: Drag files here or click to select

errors.noJsonl: No .jsonl files were found in the uploaded content

codex.description: Bring existing Codex sessions into the dashboard. User messages, assistant output, token snapshots, tool calls, and waiting/active lifecycle state are reconstructed from the original rollout JSONL files using the same pipeline as real-time monitoring.
codex.scopeNote: This import processes only {{provider}} transcripts. It never changes your Claude Code history or Codex CLI configuration.
codex.accuracyNote: Re-running is safe. Imported rollout cursors are retained, so already-accounted token deltas and tool calls are never added twice.
codex.stepLocateBody: Codex stores each session as an append-only rollout JSONL file under the sessions folder. Its nested date folders are scanned automatically.
codex.stepArchiveBody: To move history from another machine, archive the sessions folder first, then copy it over (AirDrop, scp, USB, cloud storage). Include session_index.jsonl too when you want native /rename titles from that machine.
codex.stepChooseBody: Rescan this machine's Codex sessions, point to a copied or extracted folder, or upload rollout files and archives directly.
codex.stepVerifyBody: After import, open Analytics → Cost to confirm the breakdown. The same rollout can always be imported again safely.
codex.defaultLocation: Default Codex sessions location on this machine
codex.modeRescanDesc: Re-read ~/.codex/sessions and import rollout history that is not in the dashboard yet.
codex.modeFolderDesc: Scan a copied or extracted Codex directory for rollout JSONL files, including nested date folders.
codex.modeUploadDesc: Drop rollout JSONL files or an archive (.zip / .tar.gz) directly into the browser.
codex.folderHelper: Absolute path. Tilde (~) is expanded. The folder and all nested date folders are scanned recursively for Codex rollout files.
codex.dropzoneHint: Drag Codex rollout files here or click to select
codex.dropzoneSub: Accepts rollout .jsonl files, session_index.jsonl, .zip, .tar, .tar.gz, .tgz, and .gz archives

alertsHub.title: Alerts
alertsHub.description: Define alert rules, route them to webhook channels, and review what has fired - all in one place.
alertsHub.rulesHint: Conditions that trigger an alert. Evaluated server-side against the live event stream.
alertsHub.rulesEmptyHint: Add a rule to start alerting on errors, inactivity, stuck agents, or token thresholds.

steps: Create or open a Slack app at api.slack.com/apps.
Turn on 'Incoming Webhooks', then click 'Add New Webhook to Workspace'.
Choose the channel to post to and authorize.
Copy the generated URL (https://hooks.slack.com/services/…) and paste it above.
Open your server → Server Settings → Integrations → Webhooks.
Click 'New Webhook', pick a channel, optionally rename it.
Click 'Copy Webhook URL' and paste it above.
In the target Teams channel, click ⋯ → 'Workflows'.
Pick the template 'Post to a channel when a webhook request is received'.
Finish the flow and copy the generated HTTP POST URL.
Paste it above. (Classic Office 365 connectors were retired in 2025 - use Workflows.)
Open the Google Chat space → space title → 'Apps & integrations'.
Click 'Webhooks' → 'Add webhook' and give it a name.
Copy the webhook URL and paste it above.
Main Menu → Integrations → Incoming Webhooks (an admin must enable webhooks first).
Click 'Add Incoming Webhook' and choose a channel.
Save, then copy the webhook URL and paste it above.
Administration → Integrations → New → Incoming.
Enable it, pick a channel, and save.
Copy the 'Webhook URL' and paste it above.
Message @BotFather, run /newbot, and copy the bot token.
Add the bot to your group/channel (or just DM it).
Find the chat ID: send a message, open https://api.telegram.org/bot<token>/getUpdates, read result[].message.chat.id.
Enter the Bot token and Chat ID above - no URL needed.
Open the target Service → Integrations → 'Add integration'.
Choose 'Events API v2'.
Copy the Integration Key (the routing key).
Enter it as the Routing key above - the Events API URL is prefilled.
Settings → Integrations → add an 'API' integration.
Copy the generated API key.
Note your account region (US or EU).
Enter the API key and region above - the alerts URL is derived from the region.
Integrations → REST Endpoint, and enable it.
Copy the REST URL - it already contains your API key.
Replace the trailing '$routing_key' with one of your routing keys.
Paste the full URL above.
Create a Zap with the trigger 'Webhooks by Zapier' → 'Catch Hook'.
Copy the custom webhook URL it gives you.
Paste it above. The alert arrives as JSON: { event, alert }.
Add a 'Webhooks' → 'Custom webhook' module as the first step of a scenario.
Click 'Add', create the hook, and copy its URL.
Paste it above, then run once so Make learns the payload shape.
Add a 'Webhook' node to your workflow; set the method to POST.
Copy the Production URL.
Activate the workflow and paste the URL above (http is allowed for self-hosted).
Create a workflow with an 'HTTP / Webhook' trigger.
Copy the unique endpoint URL.
Paste it above; inspect deliveries in the Pipedream event inspector.
Point this at any endpoint that accepts a JSON POST (https, or http for local testing).
Body shape: { event: 'alert.triggered', source, sent_at, alert: { … } }.
Optional: set a signing secret (HMAC-SHA256 over the body → X-Webhook-Signature header) and custom headers.
Tip: use a free inspector like webhook.site to see the exact payload.

remoteSources.title: Remote Data Sources
remoteSources.description: Collect Claude Code and Codex usage from other machines over SSH - e.g. a dev box or cloud VM you drive over SSH while running this dashboard locally. Authentication uses your own SSH setup (~/.ssh/config, keys, agent); no passwords are stored here.
remoteSources.scopeDesc: Choose which machines' data the whole dashboard shows. Changes apply immediately across every page — sessions, analytics, and cost.
remoteSources.scopeAllDesc: This machine plus every configured remote source, combined.
remoteSources.scopeLocalDesc: Only sessions collected locally — hides all remote-source data.
remoteSources.scopeSelectedDesc: Pick exactly which machines to include, below.
remoteSources.fieldRemoteHomeHint: Linux/macOS: default ~/.claude (or an absolute path like /home/you/.claude). Windows SSH + Claude in WSL: leave blank (auto-detect) or use wsl:~/.claude. Native Windows: C:/Users/you/.claude.
remoteSources.fieldRemoteCodexHomeHint: Defaults to ~/.codex and imports its sessions plus native renamed titles. For Windows SSH with Codex in WSL, leave blank (auto-detect) or use wsl:~/.codex.
remoteSources.emptyHint: Add a machine you reach over SSH to pull its Claude Code and Codex usage in.
remoteSources.sessionCountHint: Sessions linked to this source (not every session visible when data scope is All)
remoteSources.purgeData: Also delete the sessions imported from this source (cannot be undone)

cursorPathsNote: Informational: Cursor sessions count here too — Cursor happens to use the same ~/.claude paths as Claude Code (locally and on synced remotes).
